Low-rank adaptation, introduced as LoRA and extended by QLoRA, starts from the observation that the update a pretrained weight matrix needs for a new task tends to have much lower intrinsic rank than the matrix itself, so instead of updating the full d×k weight matrix W0 during fine-tuning, LoRA freezes W0 and learns a decomposition ΔW = BA, where B has shape d×r and A has shape r×k with r much smaller than min(d,k), so the forward pass becomes h = W0x + (α/r)BAx and only A and B receive gradients, cutting trainable parameters from dk to r(d+k).
QLoRA pushes this further by quantizing the frozen base weights to 4-bit precision (using a normal-float NF4 scheme and double quantization of the quantization constants themselves), keeping the small LoRA adapters in higher precision such as bf16, and backpropagating through the quantized weights via on-the-fly dequantization, which lets a 65-billion-parameter model be instruction-tuned on a single consumer-class GPU.
The practical payoff is that many task-specific adapters can be trained and swapped cheaply against one shared frozen backbone, but the approach is sensitive to the choice of rank r and target layers, can underperform full fine-tuning when the task genuinely requires a high-rank shift in behavior, and introduces additional quantization noise that can degrade calibration on out-of-distribution prompts.

Direct Preference Optimization addresses a different pain point in the standard reinforcement-learning-from-human-feedback pipeline, where a separate reward model must be trained and then used to drive an unstable, sample-heavy PPO loop against a policy while penalizing divergence from a reference model.
The RLHF objective maximizes the expected reward E[r(x,y)] minus a KL penalty β·KL(π‖π_ref) between the policy π and reference π_ref, and this objective has a closed-form optimal solution π*(y|x) = (1/Z(x))·π_ref(y|x)·exp(r(x,y)/β), where Z(x) is a per-prompt normalizing constant; inverting this expression gives the reward implied by any policy as r(x,y) = β·log(π*(y|x)/π_ref(y|x)) + β·log Z(x).
Substituting this reward into the Bradley-Terry preference probability p(y_w ≻ y_l|x) = σ(r(x,y_w) − r(x,y_l)) makes the intractable log Z(x) term cancel between the winning and losing completions, yielding the DPO loss L(θ) = −E[log σ(β·log(π_θ(y_w|x)/π_ref(y_w|x)) − β·log(π_θ(y_l|x)/π_ref(y_l|x)))], which is optimized directly by supervised gradient descent on preference pairs with no reward model and no on-policy sampling.
This made preference-based alignment far cheaper and more stable to run, but it is an offline method that can only re-weight behavior already present in the reference model's distribution, is sensitive to the quality of that reference policy, and is known to exhibit a length bias where longer completions are implicitly favored.

Group Relative Policy Optimization emerged from reasoning-focused post-training, where the goal is to reinforce chain-of-thought behavior using automatically verifiable rewards such as correctness on math problems or passing unit tests, and where PPO's usual learned value network doubles the memory and compute cost by requiring a second model roughly the size of the policy.
GRPO removes that critic by sampling a group of G completions per prompt from the current policy, scoring each with a scalar reward r_i, and computing a group-relative advantage A_i = (r_i − mean(r_1,…,r_G)) / std(r_1,…,r_G) in place of a learned baseline, then optimizing a PPO-style clipped objective J(θ) = E[(1/G)Σ_i min(ρ_i·A_i, clip(ρ_i, 1−ε, 1+ε)·A_i)] − β·KL(π_θ‖π_ref), where ρ_i is the importance ratio π_θ(o_i|q)/π_old(o_i|q) and the KL term is subtracted directly rather than folded into the reward.
This design underlies self-improving reasoning training such as DeepSeek's math and R1-style models, letting long chains of thought be reinforced purely from outcome correctness, but it is vulnerable to reward hacking on gameable verifiers, degenerates when every sample in a group receives the same reward so the standard deviation collapses toward zero, and multiplies rollout cost by the group size G.

Sparse Mixture-of-Experts architectures, popularized in this window by Mixtral, tackle a scaling problem rather than an alignment one: dense transformer feed-forward layers tie total parameter count directly to per-token compute, so growing capacity always grows inference cost.
An MoE layer replaces the single feed-forward block with N expert feed-forward networks and a router that computes gate logits g = softmax(W_g x) and activates only the top-k highest-scoring experts per token (k=2 of 8 in Mixtral), producing an output y = Σ_{i∈top-k} g_i·FFN_i(x) after renormalizing the selected gates to sum to one, so only a small active-parameter subset is used per token even though the full expert set is stored.
Training such routers requires an auxiliary load-balancing loss, typically of the form L_aux = N·Σ_i f_i·P_i, where f_i is the fraction of tokens sent to expert i and P_i is the router's average probability mass on that expert, which discourages the router from collapsing onto a few favored experts.
This lets models like Mixtral match or exceed larger dense models while activating far fewer parameters per token, but the full expert set must still reside in memory, distributed training must contend with load imbalance across devices, and routing instability or expert collapse remains an open engineering challenge, alongside the added difficulty of quantizing a model whose behavior is sensitive to router precision.
